label: gs-zebot-locomotion
topic: Zebot engineering and locomotion: biohybrid swimmers/biobots, larval zebrafish swimming kinematics and scaling, and candidate Lean-statable laws with open data
summary:
Harvested 20 papers; 19 DOIs resolved through Crossref and/or Europe PMC with matching titles, and 15 abstracts were opened for numbers. One DOI (Fuiman & Webb 1988) did not resolve and is listed in could_not_find. Nothing was run beyond metadata/abstract fetches; no full texts were opened, so all numbers are abstract-level.

Most useful result for Lean: van Leeuwen, Voesenek & Muller 2015 gives a complete numeric tuple for larval zebrafish (frequency 80-95 Hz, tail amplitude 1.8-2.4 mm, Re 60 to 1400, St 2.5 falling to 0.72, versus 0.2-0.6 for large swimmers). This supports three statements: (1) St = f*A/v as a definitional identity; (2) St is monotonically decreasing in Re across the larval range; (3) larval St lies strictly above the adult band 0.2-0.6. My own arithmetic check on the abstract numbers: f*A = 95 Hz * 2.4 mm = 228 mm/s; with St 0.72 that implies v about 317 mm/s, and with a body length near 4 mm (my assumption, not in the abstract) in water Re is about 1270, the same order as the reported 1400.

Other candidate laws: (4) viscous/inertial regime threshold for coasting zebrafish, viscous at Re < 300 and inertial at Re > 1000 (McHenry & Lauder 2005); (5) frequency band law, 2-20 Hz below a 0.5-1 m crossover and f inversely proportional to length above it (Sanchez-Rodriguez et al. 2023, about 1200 individuals, open access) - larval zebrafish at up to 100 Hz sit outside the 2-20 Hz band, a useful falsification target; (6) speed scales as length times frequency (same paper; Bainbridge 1958); (7) Gazzola et al. 2014 swimming-number scaling; (8) low-Re time-irreversibility (Purcell 1977) as the design constraint for biohybrid flagellar swimmers (Williams 2014, Aydin 2019).

Biobot numbers from abstracts: anthrobots 30-500 micron diameter and 5-50 micron/s; cardiomyocyte flagellar swimmer 5-10 micron/s (one tail) and 81 micron/s (two tails); tissue-engineered ray at 1/10 scale. Xenobot abstracts give no speeds.

Caveats: the Gazzola 2014 and Sanchez-Rodriguez 2023 compilations span many animal groups and must be filtered against holdout/split.json before any use; I did not open either dataset. Gazzola, Bainbridge and Purcell have no abstract in Europe PMC, so the laws attributed to them are from my memory of the papers, with only the title/DOI verified. I did not confirm which papers deposit raw kinematic data. Working files are in D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/gs-zebot-locomotion/ (dois.txt, show.py, epmc/*.json raw responses).

findings.claim: Larval zebrafish Strouhal number falls nonlinearly from 2.5 to 0.72 as Reynolds number rises from 60 to 1400; large swimmers sit at 0.2-0.6.
findings.evidence_quote: decreases nonlinearly towards values of large swimmers (0.2-0.6)

findings.claim: Larval zebrafish at 4-5 dpf reach higher tail-beat frequency and amplitude than at 2 dpf.
findings.evidence_quote: reach higher f (95 Hz) and Atail (2.4 mm) than at 2 dpf (80 Hz, 1.8 mm)

findings.claim: Larval zebrafish (2-21 dpf) sustain tail-beat frequencies up to 100 Hz in cyclic swimming; strain up to 0.19, strain rate up to 120 per s; body-wave to curvature-wave length ratio 1:1.2.
findings.evidence_quote: fish larvae maintain tail beat frequencies of up to 100 Hz
findings.value: f max 100 Hz; strain 0.19; strain rate 120 s^-1; phase shift 57-63 degrees

findings.claim: Zebrafish coasting has a viscous regime below Re 300 (larvae and juveniles) and an inertial regime above Re 1000 (adults), with adult inertial drag coefficient about 0.024.
findings.evidence_quote: We found a viscous regime at Re < 300

findings.claim: Simulated 3 and 5 dpf zebrafish larvae: raising body-wave amplitude raises speed from 7 to 21 body lengths per second and propulsive efficiency from 0.22 to 0.32 while power quadruples.
findings.evidence_quote: increased forward swimming speed from 7 to 21 body lengths per second
findings.confidence: high (abstract opened); simulation, not direct measurement

findings.claim: Across about 1200 undulatory swimmers, frequency is tuned in 2-20 Hz below a 0.5-1 m size crossover and is inversely proportional to length above it; predicted top speed 5-10 m/s.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-41368-6 (open access; abstract via Europe PMC, PMID 37689714)
findings.evidence_quote: the frequency can be tuned between 2-20 Hz due to biological constraints
findings.value: n~1200; crossover 0.5-1 m; 2-20 Hz; f ~ 1/L above; v max 5-10 m/s
findings.confidence: high for the abstract; dataset not opened and spans many animal groups, so filter against the holdout split before use

findings.claim: Larval fish swim in the intermediate hydrodynamic regime between viscous and inertial flow and shift toward inertial as they grow and speed up.
findings.evidence_quote: larval fish operate in the intermediate hydrodynamic regime

findings.claim: Larval zebrafish (6-9 days old) have two swim categories (burst and slow) and two turn categories (escape and routine); about 200 neurons project from brainstem to spinal cord.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.203.17.2565 (abstract via Europe PMC, PMID 10934000; Crossref lookup failed, DOI matched in Europe PMC)
findings.evidence_quote: Swimming episodes appeared to fall into two categories
findings.value: 2 swim types, 2 turn types, ~200 descending neurons

findings.claim: Unsupervised clustering of millions of larval zebrafish swim bouts yields thirteen basic swimming patterns.
findings.evidence_quote: We identified a set of thirteen basic swimming patterns
findings.confidence: high (abstract opened); data deposit location not checked

findings.claim: Larval zebrafish swim in discrete bouts separated by longer rests, modelled as marked renewal processes dependent on hunger state.
findings.evidence_quote: Zebrafish larvae swim in punctuated bouts separated by longer periods of rest

findings.claim: Anthrobots are self-constructing human-lung-cell biobots 30-500 microns across that move by cilia at 5-50 microns per second.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202303575 (open access; abstract via Europe PMC, PMID 38032125)
findings.value: diameter 30-500 um; speed 5-50 um/s; 2 weeks culture
findings.confidence: high (abstract opened; Crossref lookup failed, DOI matched in Europe PMC, which lists year 2024)

findings.claim: Xenobots are designed in silico by AI and built from frog cells; later versions self-organize and move by surface cilia without scaffolds.
findings.evidence_quote: These xenobots exhibit coordinated locomotion via cilia present on their surface
findings.value: no speeds given in either abstract
findings.confidence: high for the qualitative claim; no kinematic numbers obtained

findings.claim: Xenobot assemblies can replicate kinematically by gathering loose cells into functional copies.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2112672118 (open access; abstract via Europe PMC, PMID 34845026)
findings.evidence_quote: moving and compressing dissociated cells in their environment into functional self-copies
findings.value: qualitative; generation counts not in abstract

findings.claim: A cardiomyocyte-driven PDMS flagellar swimmer self-propels at low Reynolds number at 5-10 microns per second; a two-tailed version reaches 81 microns per second.
findings.evidence_quote: demonstrate a two-tailed swimmer swimming at 81

findings.claim: A tissue-engineered ray built from rat cardiomyocytes on an elastomer body with a gold skeleton swims by undulation at 1/10 scale and is steered by light.
findings.evidence_quote: we replicated fish morphology at 1/10 scale
findings.value: 1/10 scale; swim speed not in abstract

findings.claim: A biohybrid fish with a muscular bilayer and an autonomous pacing node shows self-sustained body-caudal-fin swimming.
findings.value: no speed or duration in abstract
findings.confidence: high for the qualitative claim (Crossref lookup failed; DOI matched in Europe PMC)

findings.claim: The medusoid, a free-swimming jellyfish analogue of rat tissue on silicone, was designed to match jellyfish stroke kinematics and fluid interactions.
findings.evidence_quote: freely swimming jellyfish from chemically dissociated rat tissue and silicone polymer

findings.claim: A biohybrid flagellar swimmer driven by on-board optogenetic neuromuscular units achieves untethered forward locomotion through time-irreversible flagellar dynamics.
findings.confidence: high (abstract opened). Note: my first guess for this DOI (10.1073/pnas.1817682116) is a different paper, a skeletal-muscle pump-bot with flow up to 22.5 microlitres per minute.

findings.claim: Gazzola, Argentina & Mahadevan propose swimming-number scaling for aquatic locomotion (Re proportional to Sw^(4/3) in the laminar regime and to Sw in the turbulent regime).
findings.value: exponents 4/3 and 1 are from my memory of the paper, not from an opened text
findings.confidence: low for the numbers (no abstract available in Europe PMC; only DOI/title verified). Dataset spans many animal groups; filter against the holdout split.

findings.claim: Bainbridge 1958 relates fish swimming speed to body size and tail-beat frequency and amplitude; Purcell 1977 sets out locomotion constraints at low Reynolds number.
findings.confidence: DOI and title verified via Crossref; content not opened, so the linear speed-frequency law and the reciprocal-motion theorem attributed to them are from memory

key_claims: Larval zebrafish St drops from 2.5 to 0.72 as Re rises from 60 to 1400, versus 0.2-0.6 in large swimmers (van Leeuwen et al. 2015).
Larval zebrafish tail-beat frequency reaches 80-100 Hz, far above the 2-20 Hz band reported for most undulatory swimmers under about 0.5-1 m.
Zebrafish coasting is viscous below Re 300 and inertial above Re 1000 (McHenry & Lauder 2005).
Cilia- and cardiomyocyte-driven biobots move at microns to tens of microns per second (anthrobots 5-50, flagellar swimmer 5-10 and 81).
19 of 20 attempted DOIs resolved; numbers for 15 come from opened abstracts, none from full text.
recommendations: Lean statement 1 (definitional): St = f*A/v, with the van Leeuwen 2015 tuple as a worked instance; first open the full text to get the measured speeds rather than my back-calculated ~317 mm/s.
Lean statement 2 (empirical, falsifiable): St is antitone in Re over Re in [60, 1400] for larval zebrafish, and St > 0.6 throughout that range.
Lean statement 3: regime predicate for coasting, viscous if Re < 300 and inertial if Re > 1000, with the 300-1000 gap left explicitly undecided.

Lean statement 4: frequency band law (2-20 Hz below the size crossover, f proportional to 1/L above) from Sanchez-Rodriguez 2023; test whether larval zebrafish violate the band, and filter the compilation against holdout/split.json before touching it.
Before any nanopub draft, open the full texts and data supplements for van Leeuwen 2015 and Sanchez-Rodriguez 2023 and confirm a downloadable table exists.
Run a separate search for zebrafish-larva-inspired soft robots; this pass found none.
lay_summary: Scientists have built tiny living robots from frog cells, human lung cells and rat heart cells; they swim very slowly, about the width of a hair every second or so.
Baby zebrafish are also tiny swimmers, and they wag their tails incredibly fast, up to about 100 times a second.
Because they are so small, water feels thick and sticky to them, so they waste more effort than big fish do; as they grow and speed up, their swimming gets more efficient.
We found published numbers for these facts in 19 papers and picked out a few simple rules that could be written as exact maths and checked against measurements.
We only read the short summaries of the papers, not the full papers, so the numbers still need a closer check.

glossary.Reynolds number (Re): A number comparing how much a swimmer's motion is ruled by its own momentum versus the stickiness of the water; small animals have low values.
glossary.Strouhal number (St): Tail-beat frequency times tail-swing width divided by swimming speed; lower values (about 0.2-0.6) mean more efficient swimming.
glossary.Swimming number (Sw): A size-and-tail-beat measure used by Gazzola and colleagues to predict swimming speed.
glossary.tail-beat frequency: How many times per second the tail swings back and forth.
glossary.amplitude: How far the tail tip swings from side to side.
glossary.viscous regime: Conditions where the water's stickiness dominates and a swimmer stops almost at once when it stops pushing.
glossary.inertial regime: Conditions where momentum dominates and a swimmer keeps gliding after it stops pushing.
glossary.intermediate regime: The in-between range where both stickiness and momentum matter.
glossary.dpf: Days post-fertilization, the age of a fish embryo or larva.
glossary.body lengths per second (BL/s): Speed measured in how many of its own lengths an animal travels each second.
glossary.biohybrid: A machine made partly of living cells and partly of man-made material.
glossary.biobot / xenobot / anthrobot: Small moving clumps of living cells built or grown to act like robots; xenobots use frog cells, anthrobots use human lung cells.
glossary.cardiomyocyte: A heart muscle cell that contracts on its own.
glossary.cilia: Tiny hair-like structures on cells that beat to push fluid.
glossary.flagellum: A whip-like tail used by very small swimmers.
glossary.time-irreversible motion: A stroke that does not look the same played backwards; needed to move forward in very sticky conditions.
glossary.optogenetic: Engineered so that cells respond to light.
glossary.PDMS: A soft silicone rubber used for the bodies of small devices.
glossary.propulsive efficiency: The share of a swimmer's effort that ends up as useful forward motion.
glossary.undulatory swimming: Swimming by sending a wave down the body.
glossary.swim bout: A short burst of swimming followed by a pause.
glossary.marked renewal process: A statistical model of events that occur at random intervals, each with a type.
glossary.DOI: A permanent identifier for a published paper.
glossary.Lean: A computer language for writing maths statements that a program can check.
glossary.monotone / antitone: Always going up / always going down as another quantity increases.
glossary.Crossref / Europe PMC: Public databases of paper records and summaries.
